notes.meaning: Paul makes a solemn promise that he is telling the truth. He calls on Christ, who sees the heart, as his witness. His conscience, guided by the Holy Spirit, agrees. He speaks so strongly because many Jews thought he had turned against his own people.
Paul carries a deep grief that never really leaves him. He does not name the cause yet, because it was painful to say. The cause is that so many of his fellow Jews were turning away from Christ.

Paul loves his people so much that he could wish to be cursed and cut off from Christ himself, if that would save them. Moses once prayed something similar for Israel (Exodus 32:32). Paul says "I could wish," not "I do wish." He knew such a trade was not possible, but his love was that strong.

Paul lists Israel's great gifts from God. God adopted them as his family. His glory, his visible presence, dwelt among them. They received the covenants (God's binding promises), the law at Sinai, the temple worship and the promises of the coming Messiah. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were their fathers. Greatest of all, Christ came from them as a man. Yet Paul calls this same Christ "God over all," a clear witness that Jesus is God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars put a full stop after "Christ," so the closing words become a separate praise to God the Father. Others answer that no manuscript supports this, and that Bible praises normally begin "Blessed be God."

notes.meaning: Israel's unbelief does not mean God's promise has failed. Being born into the nation of Israel does not make someone part of the true Israel that God's promise is about. As one writer puts it, grace does not run in the blood.

differ.view: The true Israel is the part of the nation that God, by his own free choice, chose for eternal salvation.
God accepts all who believe, and only them. The true Israel is the believers, not everyone born a Jew.

notes.meaning: Even in Abraham's own family, not every son was counted for the promise. God said the promised line would come through Isaac, not through Ishmael. So physical descent from Abraham was never enough by itself.

God's true children are not simply Abraham's natural descendants. They are the "children of the promise," people who exist because God promised it, as Isaac did. Isaac is often seen as a picture of true believers, born by God's power rather than human strength.

God promised Abraham that at the set time he would return and Sarah would have a son. Sarah was far too old to have children. Isaac was born because God's word made it happen, not through natural power.

Paul gives an even clearer example. Rebecca's twins had the same father and the same mother. Before they were born or had done anything good or bad, God said the older (Esau) would serve the younger (Jacob). God made this choice (often called "election") so that it would rest on God who calls, not on anything they did.

differ.view: God freely chose Jacob before birth, with no regard to works done or foreseen. This shows how God chooses particular people for salvation.
The words are about two nations and their privileges on earth, not about anyone's eternal destiny. Esau himself never served Jacob, but his descendants, the Edomites, served Israel.

notes.meaning: Paul quotes Malachi, who was speaking of the nations that came from the two brothers, Israel and Edom. In Bible speech, "hated" often means "loved less" or "not chosen for the same blessings," as when Jesus says to "hate" father and mother. God gave Israel blessings he did not give Edom.

differ.view: The earthly blessings were signs of something deeper: God's free love and spiritual favor toward Jacob.
The verse speaks of the two peoples. It is not about the persons of Jacob and Esau, nor about their eternal state.

notes.meaning: Paul expects someone to ask whether God is unfair to choose this way. His answer is strong: certainly not! The Judge of all the earth always does right.

God told Moses he will have mercy on whom he chooses to have mercy. He said this while showing Moses his goodness, so it is a word about God's kindness. No one deserves mercy, so God is free to give it as he wills.

differ.view: God shows mercy by his own free choice. There is no cause outside himself for why he favors some and not others.
God shows mercy on the terms he himself has set: to those who believe in his Son.

notes.meaning: Salvation does not come from human wanting or human effort ("running"). It comes from God, who shows mercy. People should still seek God earnestly, but their seeking earns no credit. All the glory goes to God's grace.

God told Pharaoh that he had raised him up to show God's power and spread God's name through all the earth. Through the plagues and the Exodus, God's name became known everywhere. Pharaoh still acted freely and chose his own stubborn course.

differ.view: God on purpose appointed Pharaoh to this role from the start, to display his power. Pharaoh was still to blame for his own evil.
God did not make Pharaoh wicked. He set on the throne a man he found already proud and stubborn, and the judgment followed because Pharaoh would not repent.

notes.meaning: Paul sums up: God has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. Pharaoh also hardened his own heart. God's hardening means giving people over to the sin they have chosen.

differ.view: By his own will God holds back softening grace from some and leaves them to their sin. Those saved must thank God alone, and those lost must blame themselves.
Those God hardens are those who refuse to believe. He leaves them to the hardness of their own hearts.

notes.meaning: Paul expects a second objection. If no one can resist God's will, why does God still blame anyone? People have raised this question in every age.

Paul answers that a creature has no right to talk back to its Creator. He uses Isaiah's picture: a clay pot does not argue with the one who shaped it. God's ways are far beyond us, and the right response is humble trust, not accusing God.

A potter has the right to take one lump of clay and make one pot for special use and another for everyday use. In the same way, God has the right to do as he sees best with his creatures. Isaiah and Jeremiah used the same picture.

differ.view: The lump is fallen humanity. No one has any claim on God, so he may show mercy to some and pass by others without wronging anyone.
God has the right to appoint believers to honor and unbelievers to dishonor. Following Jeremiah's potter, the picture speaks of how God deals with nations.

notes.meaning: Paul asks: what if God, wanting to show his anger against sin and his power, put up with great patience with people headed for destruction? And what if he did this to show the riches of his glory to people he prepared for glory? God's long patience shows his kindness even toward those who deserve judgment. Paul says plainly that God himself prepares his people for glory.

differ.view: Both groups rest in God's secret plan (Calvin). Many Reformed writers also stress that sinners fit themselves for destruction, while God prepares his people for heaven.
The "vessels of wrath" are those who keep rejecting God's mercy. They are made fit for destruction by their own stubborn unbelief, as Pharaoh and the unbelieving Jews of Paul's day were.

notes.meaning: Paul tells us who these people of mercy are: "us," the ones God has called. They come not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (non-Jewish peoples). Here, for the first time in the chapter, Paul brings in the calling of the Gentiles.

Paul quotes Hosea: God will call "My people" those who were not his people, and "Beloved" those who were not loved. Hosea first spoke of the northern tribes of Israel, who had sunk to the level of the pagan nations. Paul rightly applies the same mercy to the Gentiles.

In the very place where people were told "You are not my people," they will be called children of the living God. They do not need to move to Jerusalem; God will claim them wherever they live. He is called the "living" God in contrast to dead idols.

Isaiah cried out that even if Israel became as many as the sand of the sea, only a remnant (a small group left over) would be saved. The Lord would carry out his judgment fully and quickly. Isaiah first spoke of judgment in his own day, but the same pattern shows it is nothing new for God to judge much of Israel while keeping his promise through a few.

Isaiah also said that if the Lord of Hosts (the Lord who commands heaven's armies) had not left a few survivors, Israel would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah. The wonder is not that many are lost, but that any are saved at all. That is all because of God's mercy.

Paul draws a surprising conclusion. The Gentiles were not chasing after being right with God, yet they received it. They received it by faith: they were justified, that is, declared right with God by trusting Christ.
Israel worked hard to follow a law meant to lead to righteousness, but they did not reach it. To become right with God by the law, a person would have to keep it perfectly, and no one can.
Why did Israel fail? They tried to gain righteousness by their own works instead of by faith. So they stumbled over the "stumbling stone," which is Christ.

differ.view: God's hidden choosing stands behind everything. Still, Israel's failure was truly their own fault, coming from pride and trust in their works.
Paul gives no hint that God decreed their failure. The reason he gives is simply that they would not seek righteousness by faith.

notes.meaning: Paul combines two sayings from Isaiah. God lays in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, and that stone is Christ. Many fall over him through unbelief. But everyone who trusts in him will never be put to shame or let down.
